A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Neural Attention Search by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. Changed models and experimental settings require care when interpreting performance differences.

before.justification: v1 reports original PG-19 training experiments, NIAH and LongBench evaluations, hyperparameter ablations, and KV-cache distribution analyses.

after.justification: v3 reports original PG-19, RULER, and LongBench results, ablations, KV-cache analyses, and measured inference latency and GPU memory usage.

M1.justification: The three token roles remain, but their learning procedure changes substantively. v1 Appendix A stabilizes mask gradients using an unmasked softmax denominator and approximates non-global-token corrections within a 16-token neighborhood; v3 Appendix C instead clips the gradient factor and omits those corrections. Section 4.2 also introduces label-focused optimization for synthetic passkey data.

E1.justification: PG-19 and LongBench coverage remains, while fine-tuning adds synthetic multiple-passkey retrieval data. The standalone NIAH evaluation is replaced by RULER's four-category synthetic evaluation, reaching 128k context for Llama and 32k for Mistral. v3 also adds inference resource tests extending to 700k tokens.

E2.justification: The LongBench comparisons retain full attention, DuoAttention, Streaming LLM, and H2O, and add SnapKV, AdaKV, ChunkKV, CriticalKV, PyramidKV, and MoA. These additions appear in v3 Tables 2 and 4–6, beyond the comparator set in v1 Tables 1–3.

E3.justification: Reported GPT-2 training changes from 120,000 to 600,000 iterations, and Streaming LLM's PG-19 settings change to eight sink tokens with revised windows. Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Gradient-1048k is replaced by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; peak fine-tuning learning rate changes from 3e-4 to 2e-3, with revised regularization choices. New protocols include pre-question eviction for one-time comparators and BF16 latency tests with 32k-token chunked prefilling.

E4.justification: The standalone needle-position robustness analysis disappears. v3 retains regularization and sliding-window sensitivity studies, but removes the Mistral regularization sweep and the W=384 condition. KV-distribution case studies also change: RepoBench-P and DuReader diagnostics disappear, while NarrativeQA and MultiNews are examined across both models.

E5.justification: v3 checklist item 7 newly states that every experiment ran once with a fixed random seed. v1 does not disclose this information. Neither version reports error bars or significance tests; the change establishes disclosure, not a reduction in repeated runs.

E6.justification: The reported PG-19 result at zero regularization changes from approximately 60% cache with slightly lower perplexity to approximately 35% with slightly higher perplexity. LongBench scores and ablation results are extensively replaced under revised settings. v3 adds RULER results and reports 1.83x prefilling and 1.38x decoding speedups at 200k tokens; these do not establish same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: Most attention-mask and gradient derivations are retained and relocated. However, the mathematical definition of the stabilizing gradient factor changes from normalization by the unmasked denominator in v1 Appendix A.1 to min(exp(A)/S, 1) in v3 Appendix C.1. v3 also explicitly derives the search-space size as 3^(LHN).

C1.justification: Both versions claim that jointly learning global, local, and sliding-window token roles reduces KV-cache requirements while largely maintaining performance, for training from scratch and fine-tuning. The revised abstract terminology and expanded supporting experiments do not materially change these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 Appendix A newly identifies a specific limitation: the column-oriented search space excludes block-sparse and slash attention patterns. Appendix F.1 also adds the hypothesis that more evenly distributed attention values explain Mistral's need for stronger regularization. The broader-impact discussion is largely retained through relocation.

D1.justification: v3 adds detailed FlashAttention forward/backward pseudocode, an implementation URL, disclosure of a dataset-generation script, and training-time information absent from v1. Fine-tuning is reported as approximately eight hours. Pretraining time is inconsistently stated as 16 hours in Appendix E.1 and 18 hours in the checklist; external code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to distinguish KV eviction, selective computation, CPU offloading, and learned sparse attention. New discussions include MoA, MoBA, Native Sparse Attention, TokenButler, and AttentionPredictor, with an explicit contrast between MoA's head-level search and NAtS's token-level search. Some earlier coverage, including Dynamic Token Pooling, is removed.

P1.justification: Gradient derivations and GPT-2 training details move from the main text into appendices, and KV-distribution discussion is consolidated there. Related work gains a separate Sparse Attention subsection; broader impact moves to an appendix, while limitations, implementation details, acknowledgements, and a checklist receive dedicated sections. This substantially reorganizes the document.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. LongBench tables expand from five to eleven columns, the paired 50%-budget table is split, the NIAH heatmaps disappear, and a latency/memory figure is added. KV-distribution figures are replaced and regrouped, while retained method diagrams are resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: v1's practical efficiency argument rests mainly on KV-cache fractions; v3 Section 4.3 directly measures prefilling and decoding latency and GPU memory, addressing an important evidential gap. Expanded comparator coverage, RULER evaluations, and implementation documentation substantially strengthen the paper. Reduced diagnostic coverage, single-run evidence, and reporting inconsistencies limit confidence, but do not outweigh the clearer empirical support for the central efficiency claim.
